deed: Prof. Marcelle Machluf of the Technion developed nanoparticles that direct a drug straight to cancer cells
title: Prof. Marcelle Machluf of the Technion developed "Nano-Ghosts" that carry treatment directly to cancer cells

trailer.text: Prof. Marcelle Machluf is a researcher at the Technion, an Israeli institution, and according to the Times of Israel she is the dean of the Faculty of Biotechnology and Food Engineering and one of the leading bioengineers in Israel.
According to the sponsored article in Haaretz, she was born in Morocco and immigrated to Israel with her mother in 1964, when she was one year old.
According to the Technion, her laboratory developed "Nano-Ghosts", tiny particles made from the outer membrane of stem cells, which can target different types of cancer.
According to the Technion, in animal experiments the system doubled life expectancy after the development of prostate cancer, and no side effects were observed.
According to the sponsored article in Haaretz, in late 2019 Machluf founded the company NanoGhost with Yonatan Malca.

glance.value: One of the 60 important historical developments in Israel, 2016

stations.title: The problem: a drug that also does harm along the way

paragraphs.text: According to a sponsored article in Haaretz, cancer is the leading cause of death in Israel among both men and women.
According to the Technion, two problems in cancer treatments are the side effects of chemotherapy and the resistance that cancer cells develop to the drugs.
According to the Technion, in current treatments the drug "leaks" on its way to the tumor.
In this way it damages healthy tissue and causes serious side effects.
According to the article in Haaretz, in recent years cancer research has focused on targeted treatments, intended to attack cancer cells and reduce damage to the rest of the body.
According to the Technion, gene therapy for cancer also has great potential, but its clinical application is very limited.
According to an article in Nature Nanotechnology, the existing ways of delivering drugs in nanoparticles are also limited.

stations.title: Marcelle Machluf: from a small apartment in Ashdod to the Technion

paragraphs.text: According to the sponsored article in Haaretz, Machluf was born in Morocco, and in 1964, when she was one year old, her mother decided to immigrate with her to Israel.
The family lived in a tiny apartment in Ashdod.
The mother and daughter shared a room, and the grandmother slept in the dining area.
Today Machluf is a researcher at the Technion.
According to the Technion, she is a world-renowned researcher in drug delivery, gene therapy, cell therapy and tissue engineering.
According to the Technion, she has published over 60 articles and book chapters.

stations.title: The idea: an empty cell, a "ghost"

paragraphs.text: According to the article, Machluf began the research that led to NanoGhost in 2010 in her Technion lab.
She said that the laboratory had a program on HIV, to create a decoy that would fool the virus.
Then she asked herself why not do the same in cancer.
According to the Technion, the Nano-Ghosts are made from the outer membrane of mesenchymal stem cells.
The cells can be produced in large quantities in the laboratory, emptied of their contents and turned into empty packages.
NanoGhost CEO Yonatan Malca described it this way: you take a stem cell, empty it and create a "ghost".

stations.title: How it works: a "Trojan horse" in the bloodstream

paragraphs.text: According to the Machluf laboratory, the Nano-Ghosts are produced by hypotonic treatment and mild homogenization that remove the cell's contents, and are then reduced in size.
According to the laboratory, they can be loaded with a drug or a therapeutic substance, during the size reduction or after it.
According to the Technion, specific genes are inserted into the empty packages.
They are then injected into the bloodstream, through which they navigate to the tumor.
Only when the genes reach the tumor do they begin to produce an anti-cancer protein.
According to the Technion, the protein also acts on adjacent cancer cells and on the blood vessels that feed the tumor.
According to the Technion, the particles do not cause immune rejection, and therefore there is no need to produce the stem cells from the patient himself.
According to Yonatan Malka, CEO and co-founder of NanoGhost, selectiveness, that is, bringing the medicine directly to the target, is the most important attribute.

stations.title: In the laboratory: the tumors shrink

paragraphs.text: According to Nature Nanotechnology in August 2013, Machluf and her colleagues at the Technion showed that Nano-Ghosts deliver treatment specifically to the tumor.
According to the Technion, an article in Nano Letters announced a breakthrough: accurate delivery of genes to the target, without viruses.
According to the abstract of the 2016 Nano Letters article, the Nano-Ghosts introduced DNA into various cancer cells, in vitro and in a living body, without side effects.
In animals they inhibited metastatic lung cancer and prostate cancer, and greatly extended survival.
According to the Technion, the system doubled the life expectancy of animals after the development of prostate cancer.
According to Machluf, the tumor shrank after just one injection.
According to Machluf, even when the cells are returned to the body empty, without a drug, they affect, for example, inflammatory systems that arise because of the cancer.
According to the Technion, in 2016 a collaboration was announced between the Technion and the NYU Langone cancer center.
The first joint study will examine whether Nano-Ghosts can deliver treatment for metastatic melanoma to the brain.
According to the Technion, the Nano-Ghost has mechanisms that slow it enough to cross the barrier that filters the blood flowing into the brain.
Each joint project will receive a two-year grant of $500,000.

stations.title: NanoGhost: from the laboratory to a company

paragraphs.text: According to the Times of Israel, Machluf set up a company as a spin-off from the Technion to commercialize the technology.
According to the sponsored article in Haaretz, NanoGhost was founded in late 2019 by Machluf and Yonatan Malca, who has experience in capital markets and company management.
According to Innovation Israel, the company was officially founded in November 2019, after a complex investor-raising process.

According to the Times of Israel, the Israeli fund aMoon invested $5 million in the company, in a round in which aMoon's own Velocity fund, intended for early-stage investments, and a private investor from the US took part.
According to the article in Haaretz, the company also received four grants from the Israel Innovation Authority.
Dorit Sokolov of aMoon Velocity said that after 10 years of research the technology is ripe for commercialization.
According to the Times of Israel, the technology has received patents in the US and Europe, and additional patents are pending in India and China.
Machluf said that pharmaceutical companies understand today that the delivery is as important as the medicine itself.

stations.title: Recognition: a torch and one of the 60 developments

paragraphs.text: According to the Times of Israel, in 2016 the Ministry of Science and Technology selected the technology as one of the 60 important historical developments in Israel.
According to the sponsored article in Haaretz, Machluf was chosen to light a torch at the ceremony marking seventy years of the State of Israel.
According to the same article, she was elected to serve as a member of the Council for Higher Education.
According to Machluf, up to the article in Innovation Israel they had worked only with animals, and methods better suited to humans still need to be found.
According to Malca in 2025, the technology is still at the preclinical stage.
Machluf said that a biological solution has a drawback: production of the cells is relatively limited, and a long time will always be needed to test and characterize the drug.
According to her, the Nano-Ghost delivery system will not be suitable for all types of drugs.
In 2021 Malca and Machluf said that much work is still needed before one can speak of a victory over cancer.
According to Machluf and Malka, the system works, and Malka added that the nano ghost reaches the cells and can be loaded with medicine.

disagreements.question: By how much did the tumors shrink in animal experiments?

versions.says: Technion: a delay of over 75% in prostate cancer and of over 50% in non-small cell lung cancer
The Machluf laboratory, on a 2013 article in Nano Letters: 80% inhibition of human prostate cancer
Malca in the article in Haaretz, 2025: in about two years, in Israel and abroad
Calcalist CTech, 2021: the hope is to reach clinical trials by 2023
Machluf in Innovation Israel: the vision is to reach clinical trials within three years

It is not known whether the patents in India and China have been granted
It is not known what the results of the joint study with NYU Langone on melanoma in the brain were
